initial_observation.encounter_context: referred to our department for purulent conjunctivitis
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Five days after his third round of chemotherapy, his Dachshund dog struck his right eye while sneezing; four hours later redness around his eye and inflammatory peri-orbital edema with fever appeared; he was unable to open his right eye upon admission 33 hours later; physical exam revealed purulent conjunctivitis with chemosis and conjunctival hyperemia of the right eye associated with inflammatory edema of both upper and lower lids, skin rupture and purulent encystment above and below his eye; white blood-cell count normal with lymphopenia; CT scan showed no intra-orbital extension; blood cultures negative; conjunctival secretions sampled for bacteriology
known_prior_history: currently treated with chemotherapy including lenalidomide and CHOP

evidence_items.source_text: Upon admission, 33 hours later, physical examination, revealed purulent conjunctivitis with chemosis and conjunctival hyperemia of the right eye associated with inflammatory edema of both the upper and lower lids. Skin rupture and purulent encystment were observed above and below his eye respectively (Figure 1A). The visual acuity was 3/10 in the right eye and 4/10 in the left eye.
The white blood-cell count was normal (4900/mm3) but the differential revealed lymphopenia (300/mm3). The absolute neutrophil count was within normal range (4400/mm3).
A computerized tomography scan revealed no evidence of intra-orbital extension (Figure 1B).

Conjunctival secretions were sampled on admission for bacteriological analysis and cultured on blood agar. Direct examination showed numerous leukocytes and rare gram-negative bacilli (Figure 1C). Regular, grey, smooth colonies grew the next day. The oxidase test was positive for the 1-3 mm diameter, non-hemolytic colonies (Figure 1D&E), strongly suggesting that the isolated strain belonged to Pasteurella genus. The involvement of Pasteurella multocida was also strongly suggested here by mannitol fermentation (API-20E Array) (Figure 1F) and confirmed by MALDI TOF mass spectrometry. The diagnosis of Pasteurella multocida conjunctivitis with pre septal-cellulitis was therefore retained.

Taking into account the animal contact and the short incubation period, suggesting the involvement of Pasteurella genus, an antibiotherapy associating amoxicillin 2 g tid and amoxicillin/clavulanate 2 g tid was administered intravenously, immediately after bacteriological sampling. No topical therapy was prescribed excepted for artificial tears. The outcome was favourable in the next three days (Figure 1G), allowing discharge of the patient with amoxicillin (2 g tid per os) alone once usual full sensitivity of Pasteurella multocida strain to amoxicillin was confirmed.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: immediately after sampling and in next three days
